# Introduction

We have several sets of data pertaining to corn seeding rate and the resulting grain yield, both in the form of GPS maps generated from precision-enabled equipment. We wish to determine the relationship between seeding rate and yield, relative to the yield that might be expected given uniform seeding. To do this, we could naively map point estimates of yield to the PGS coordinates associated with corn seeding, each seeding point tagged with a GPS coordinate and two relevant variables - `Control Rate` and `Applied Rate`. In each case, yield and seeding, estimates are taken a one second intervals on GPS precision ag enabled equipment as the seeder tractor or combine travels through a cropland.

However, we recognize that each point represents a rectangle - the rectangle that is 'swept' in the interval. So, instead of using point estimates for yield, we estimate yield over an area represented by each seeding sample. Our general algorithm is first, for each seeding data point, estimate the area seeded using trigonometric relationships between the seeding variables `Heading`, which represents the direction the seeder is traveling, and `Distance`, which represents the distance traveled since the last measurement point (thus, determines the height or length of the seeded rectangle. 

We include the variable `SwathWidth`, which represents the effective width of the seeding implement, thus the width of the seeded rectangle. More details of estimating `SwathWidth` is documented in `EffectiveSwathWidth`. The variables `Heading`, `Distance` and `Swathwidth` are used to find the corners of the seeded rectangle in a Cartesian coordinate system common to multiple seeding and yield maps, mapped by metric distance from a common origin, by the variables `Easting` and `Northing`.

Yield data are determined for each rectangle by first find a neighborhood of the original seeding data point; this will typically be twice the `SwathWidth` in each coordinate direction. The yield points are then fit to basis splines using a generalized additive model from the `mgcv` package in R. We then use Monte Carlo integration to provide an estimate of yield for the rectangle. This process is documented in more detail in `MappingYield`.

In this document, we consider two years (2018 and 2020) of variable rate seeding in corn for several fields from a farm in eastern South Dakota. We include both the the seeding rate and harvest yield for a single growing season along with prior years harvest, mapped to a common seeding rate map. We then compare the relationship between seeding rate and grain yield to the grain yield for, say 2017 (and prior years) to the yield for 2018, and ask the question - which variable seems to have the strongest correlation with yields for 2018 and 2020? We also ask the question - can we determine the effectiveness of variable seeding rate using Bayesian networks?

We use `gam` to fit a trend surface to estimate yields from different yield maps; see `MappingYield.Rmd`. Since this involves numeric integration and can be somewhat time consuming, we put save results to an `Rda` file and compute estimates only if not already available.

Sometimes the neighborhoods are too small for `gam` fits, so I've written a function to wrap the numerical integration in a try-catch block and return null if the area can't be estimated.


```{r}
areal.yield.estimate <- function(row, dat, swathwidth) {
  neighborhood <- find.neighborhood(row$Row, dat, swathwidth)
  surface.gam <- NULL
  res <- NA
  tryCatch(surface.gam <- gam(Yield ~ s(Easting,Northing), data=neighborhood), error= function(e){e})
  if(!is.null(surface.gam)) {
      res = numerical.integration.yield(row$Row,surface.gam)$Estimate
  }
  return(res)
}
```

```{r,echo=FALSE}
library(mgcv)
if(!file.exists("seeding2018.Rda")) {
  seeding2018.dat$Y18 <- NA
  seeding2018.dat$Y17 <- NA
  seeding2018.dat$Y16 <- NA
  seeding2018.dat$Y15 <- NA
  rows <- dim(seeding2018.dat)[1]
  for(row in 1:rows) {
    current <- seeding2018.dat[row,]
    current <- add.corners(current)
    #add 2018 yield estimates
    seeding2018.dat$Y18[row] <- areal.yield.estimate(current, harvest2018.dat, SwathWidth)
    seeding2018.dat$Y17[row] <- areal.yield.estimate(current, harvest2017.dat, SwathWidth)
    seeding2018.dat$Y16[row] <- areal.yield.estimate(current, harvest2016.dat, SwathWidth)
    seeding2018.dat$Y15[row] <- areal.yield.estimate(current, harvest2015.dat, SwathWidth)
  } 

  
  save(seeding2018.dat, file="seeding2018.Rda")
} else {
  load(file="seeding2018.Rda")
}
seeding2018.dat$AR18 <- seeding2018.dat$AppliedRate/1000
```
Now we consider the relationships among seeding rate and seed yield for 2018, and combined this with yield for 2017. We do this first sequentially in time for models denoted A and B as single regression models. Model A describes the relationship between seed yield for 2017, and the subsequent seeding rate for 2018, while model B describes the relationship between seeding rate for 2018 and the subsequent seed yield for 2018.

Model C is a multiple regression model that includes both seeding rate for 2018 and seed yield from 2017 and their combined effects on seed yield for 2018. An alternative version of model C (C alt) simply changes the order of the two terms in the model; this will allow us to compare two different decompositions of sums of squares in an analysis of variance so we can judge the relative weight of the two effects on seed yield.

Model D adds an iteration term to model C.

Model E does not include an interaction term but include the additive effects of prior years yields, corn from 2016 and soybean from 2015.

```{r}
modelA2018.lm <- lm(AR18 ~ Y17, data=seeding2018.dat)
modelB2018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ AR18,data=seeding2018.dat)
modelC2018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ Y17 + AR18,data=seeding2018.dat)
modelCalt2018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ AR18 + Y17,data=seeding2018.dat)
modelD2018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ Y17 + AR18 + Y17:AR18,data=seeding2018.dat)
modelE2018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ Y17 + AR18 + Y16 + Y15,data=seeding2018.dat)

modelA32018.lm <- lm(AR18 ~ poly(Y17,5), data=seeding2018.dat)
modelB32018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ poly(AR18,5), data=seeding2018.dat)
modelC32018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ poly(Y17,5) + poly(AR18,5), data=seeding2018.dat)
modelC3alt2018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ poly(AR18,5) + poly(Y17,5), data=seeding2018.dat)
modelD32018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ poly(Y17,5) + poly(AR18,5) + poly(Y17,5):poly(AR18,5), data=seeding2018.dat)
modelE32018.lm <- lm(Y18 ~ poly(Y17,5) + poly(AR18,5) + poly(Y16,5) + poly(Y15,5), data=seeding2018.dat)
  
modelAs2018.gam <- gam(AR18 ~ s(Y17), data=seeding2018.dat)
modelBs2018.gam <- gam(Y18 ~ s(AR18),data=seeding2018.dat)
modelCs2018.gam <- gam(Y18 ~ s(Y17) + s(AR18),data=seeding2018.dat)

modelDs2018.gam <- gam(Y18 ~ s(Y17) + s(AR18)+s(Y17,AR18),data=seeding2018.dat)
modelEs2018.gam <- gam(Y18 ~ s(Y17) + s(AR18) + s(Y16) + s(Y15),data=seeding2018.dat)
```

## Average Yield

There is an hidden variable in these data - the inherent fertility of the field. This fertility can be due to variations in soil type and elevation, among other geographical features. We can't measure this field directly, we can only infer it's effects on yield. This field may also vary from year to year, and from crop to crop. We wish to include an estimate of this variable in our modeling, so we take the average of several years of yield data, using only those years when seeding and other crop inputs was uniform - in our case, we expect variable rate seeding to influence the interaction of field fertility with crop. 

Since we have crops with yields on different scales, we normalize each year by calculating both mean and standard deviation of all yield estimates, then converting yield observations to a $z$-score, based on the formula $z_{i} = (y{i} - \bar y)\ \mu_y$. We then combine the averages of the $z$ scores in the variable `AVG`.

Since we have only three years of prior data for the 2018 seeding, we include the average from prior years for the analysis of 2020 seeding data; we denote this model F.

For reference, we also calculate the average yield for each year, by taking the average of all yield estimates from the original data. There is some degree of overlap in seeding rectangles, so the average of areal yield estimates mapped to the 2020 seeding map may produce a biased estimate. Note that the new variable `AVG` is an average associated with a seeding map rectangle.

```{r}
mean(harvest2015.dat$Yield,na.rm=TRUE)
mean(harvest2016.dat$Yield,na.rm=TRUE)
mean(harvest2017.dat$Yield,na.rm=TRUE)
mean(harvest2018.dat$Yield,na.rm=TRUE)
mean(harvest2019.dat$Yield,na.rm=TRUE)
mean(harvest2020.dat$Yield,na.rm=TRUE)
mean(harvest2020.dat$Yield,na.rm=TRUE)
mean(seeding2018.dat$AppliedRate,na.rm=TRUE)
mean(seeding2020.dat$AppliedRate,na.rm=TRUE)
```

```{r}
normalize <- function(x) {
  std <- sd(x)
  return (x - mean(x))/std
}
yield.dat <- seeding2020.dat[, c("Y19","Y18","Y17","Y16","Y15")]
means <- apply(yield.dat,2,normalize)
plot(yield.dat$Y19,seeding2020.dat$Y19)
seeding2020.dat$AVG <- apply(means,1,mean)
```

```{r}
modelA2020.lm <- lm(AR20 ~ Y19, data=seeding2020.dat)

modelC2020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ Y19 + AR20,data=seeding2020.dat)
modelCalt2020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ AR20 + Y19,data=seeding2020.dat)
modelD2020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ Y19 + AR20 + Y19:AR20,data=seeding2020.dat)
modelE2020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ Y19 + AR20 + Y18 + Y17 + Y16 + Y15,data=seeding2020.dat)
modelF2020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ AR20 + AVG,data=seeding2020.dat)

modelA32020.lm <- lm(AR20 ~ poly(Y19,3), data=seeding2020.dat)
modelB32020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ poly(AR20,3), data=seeding2020.dat)
modelC32020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ poly(Y19,3) + poly(AR20,3), data=seeding2020.dat)
modelC3alt2020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ poly(AR20,3) + poly(Y19,3), data=seeding2020.dat)
modelD32020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ poly(Y19,3) + poly(AR20,3) + poly(Y19,3):poly(AR20,3), data=seeding2020.dat)
modelE32020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ poly(Y19,3) + poly(AR20,3) + poly(Y18,3) +poly(Y17,3) + poly(Y16,3) + poly(Y15,3), data=seeding2020.dat)
modelF32020.lm <- lm(Y20 ~ AR20 + poly(AVG,3),data=seeding2020.dat)

modelAs2020.gam <- gam(AR20 ~ s(Y19), data=seeding2020.dat)
modelBs2020.gam <- gam(Y20 ~ s(AR20),data=seeding2020.dat)
modelCs2020.gam <- gam(Y20 ~ s(Y19) + s(AR20),data=seeding2020.dat)
modelCsalt2020.gam <- gam(Y20 ~ s(AR20) + s(Y19) ,data=seeding2020.dat)
modelDs2020.gam <- gam(Y20 ~ s(Y19) + s(AR20)+s(Y19,AR20),data=seeding2020.dat)
modelEs2020.gam <- gam(Y20 ~ s(Y19) + s(AR20) + s(Y18) + s(Y17) + s(Y16) + s(Y15), data=seeding2020.dat)
modelFs2020.gam <- gam(Y20 ~ s(AR20) + s(AVG),data=seeding2020.dat)
```

# Bayesian Network

```{r}
model1.18.dat <- seeding2018.dat[,c('Y18','AR18','Y17')]

model1.18.dag <- model2network("[Y17][AR18][Y18|AR18:Y17]")
model2.18.dag <- model2network("[Y17][AR18|Y17][Y18|AR18]")
model3.18.dag <- model2network("[Y17][AR18|Y17][Y18|Y17:AR18]")

model1.18.fit <- bn.fit(model1.18.dag, model1.18.dat)
model1.18.fit
model2.18.fit <- bn.fit(model2.18.dag, model1.18.dat)
model2.18.fit
model3.18.fit <- bn.fit(model3.18.dag, model1.18.dat)
model3.18.fit

arc.strength(model1.18.dag, model1.18.dat)
arc.strength(model1.18.dag, model1.18.dat, criterion = 'aic-g')
arc.strength(model1.18.dag, model1.18.dat, criterion = 'bic-g')
```

## Seeding and yield plots

To visualize yield more distinctly, we convert absolute yield values to ranks, and color points according to rank. This enhances the fine structure of yield in the field.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
harvest2017.dat$YieldRank <- rank(harvest2017.dat$Yield)
harvest2017.dat$YieldRank <- harvest2017.dat$YieldRank/max(harvest2017.dat$YieldRank)
seeding2018.dat$Y17Rank <- rank(seeding2018.dat$Y17)
seeding2018.dat$Y17Rank <- seeding2018.dat$Y17Rank/max(seeding2018.dat$Y17Rank)
seeding2018.dat$Y18Rank <- rank(seeding2018.dat$Y18)
seeding2018.dat$Y18Rank <- seeding2018.dat$Y18Rank/max(seeding2018.dat$Y18Rank)
seeding2018.dat$RateRank <- rank(seeding2018.dat$AR18)
seeding2018.dat$RateRank <- seeding2018.dat$RateRank/max(seeding2018.dat$RateRank)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE}
seeding2020.dat$Y15Rank <- seeding2020.dat$Y15Rank/max(seeding2020.dat$Y15Rank)

seeding2020.dat$Y16Rank <- rank(seeding2020.dat$Y16)
seeding2020.dat$Y16Rank <- seeding2020.dat$Y16Rank/max(seeding2020.dat$Y16Rank)

seeding2020.dat$Y18Rank <- seeding2020.dat$Y18Rank/max(seeding2020.dat$Y18Rank)

seeding2020.dat$Y19Rank <- seeding2020.dat$Y19Rank/max(seeding2020.dat$Y19Rank)
```

```{r,fig.width=6,fig.height=6}
Maps18 <- data.frame(Easting=c(seeding2018.dat$Easting, seeding2018.dat$Easting, seeding2018.dat$Easting),
                   Northing=c(seeding2018.dat$Northing,seeding2018.dat$Northing,seeding2018.dat$Northing),
                   Value=c(seeding2018.dat$Y17Rank,seeding2018.dat$Y18Rank,seeding2018.dat$RateRank),
                   Map=c(rep('Yield 2017',length(seeding2018.dat$Y17Rank)),
                         rep('Yield 2018',length(seeding2018.dat$Y18Rank)),
                         rep('Seeding 2018',length(seeding2018.dat$RateRank))))
ggplot(Maps18, aes(Easting,Northing)) + 
geom_point(aes(colour = Value),size=0.5) + 
scale_colour_gradient2(low=vermillion, mid=yellow, high=blue, midpoint = 0.5) +
labs(colour = "Relative Rank", x="Easting", y="Northing", title = "Yield and Seeding Maps") + facet_wrap(~ Map,nrow=2)
```

```{r,fig.width=10,fig.height=5}
GridLong <- reshape(seeding2020.dat, 
  varying = c('Y19','Y18','Y17','Y16','Y15'), 
  v.names = "Yield",
  timevar = "Year", 
  times = c(2019,2018,2017,2016,2015), 
  direction = "long")

ggplot(GridLong, aes(Yield,Y20,color=Year, alpha=0.1)) + scale_colour_manual(values=cbPalette) +
geom_point(size=2) + geom_smooth(se = FALSE,color="black") + facet_wrap(~ Year,scales = "free_x")
```

```{r}
if(!file.exists('seeding2018AStan.Rda')) {
  modelA2018.brms <- brm(Y18 ~ AR18, data=seeding2018.dat)
  modelB2018.brms <- brm(Y18 ~ Y17,data=seeding2018.dat)
  modelC2018.brms <- brm(Y18 ~ Y17 + AR18,data=seeding2018.dat)
  
  modelA32018.brms <- brm(Y18 ~ poly(AR18,3), data=seeding2018.dat)
  modelB32018.brms <- brm(Y18 ~ poly(Y17,3),data=seeding2018.dat)
  modelC32018.brms <- brm(Y18 ~ poly(Y17,3) + poly(AR18,3),data=seeding2018.dat)
  
  modelAs2018.brms <- brm(Y18 ~ s(AR18), data=seeding2018.dat)
  modelBs2018.brms <- brm(Y18 ~ s(Y17),data=seeding2018.dat)
  modelCs2018.brms <- brm(Y18 ~ s(Y17) + s(AR18),data=seeding2018.dat)
  save(modelA2018.brms,modelB2018.brms,modelC2018.brms,
       modelA32018.brms,modelB32018.brms,modelC32018.brms,
       modelAs2018.brms,modelBs2018.brms,modelCs2018.brms,file='seeding2018AStan.Rda')
} else {
  load(file='seeding2018AStan.Rda')
}

summary(modelA2018.brms)
plot(modelA2018.brms)
summary(modelB2018.brms)
plot(modelB2018.brms)
summary(modelC2018.brms)

summary(modelA32018.brms)
plot(modelA32018.brms)
summary(modelB32018.brms)
plot(modelB32018.brms)
summary(modelC32018.brms)
plot(modelC32018.brms)

summary(modelAs2018.brms)
plot(modelAs2018.brms)
summary(modelBs2018.brms)
plot(modelBs2018.brms)
summary(modelCs2018.brms)
plot(modelCs2018.brms)
```
